Four American Doolittle Raid bomber crewmen, who crash landed their B-25 bomber in China, are escorted through a village before being reunited with their unit. China. 1942

The Doolittle Raid, on Saturday, April 18, 1942, was an air raid by the US on the Japanese capital Tokyo during WW2, the first air strike to strike the Japanese Home Islands. It demonstrated that Japan itself was vulnerable to American air attack and provided an important boost to American morale. The raid was planned and led by Lt. Col. Jimmy Doolittle of the USAF.

Sixteen B-25B Mitchell medium bombers were launched without fighter escort from the U.S. Navy's aircraft carrier USS Hornet deep in the Western Pacific Ocean, each with a crew of five men. The plan called for them to bomb military targets in Japan, and to continue westward to land in China. Fifteen aircraft reached China, but all crashed, while the 16th landed at Vladivostok in the Soviet Union. All but three of the 80 crew members initially survived the mission. Eight airmen were captured by the Japanese Army in China; three of those were later executed. The B-25 that landed in the Soviet Union was confiscated and its crew interned for more than a year. Fourteen complete crews, except for one crewman who was killed in action, returned either to the United States or to American forces.
